strengths: Addresses a timely and important question: whether action-conditioned video world models can serve as simulators for offline robot policy evaluation, a problem largely unexplored in the OPE literature

Well-motivated observation that a single world model (unlike single-task dynamics models in model-based RL) can amortize across many tasks and policies, and the formulation cleanly situates WPE in the multi-task POMDP / OPE framework

Practical inference scheme (Blockwise-Autoregressive Diffusion Transformer with adjustable context/horizon lengths) that enables hundreds of interactive rollout steps while mitigating error accumulation, building sensibly on Diffusion Forcing

Thoughtful evaluation methodology: proposing action-conditioned agreement metrics (semantic MSE via segmentation/tracking, overall MSE, LPIPS, SSIM) validated against human judgments, which is a genuinely new evaluation angle for action-conditioned video generation

Comprehensive empirical study spanning a handcrafted simulator (LIBERO), multiple real robot morphologies from OpenX, ablations on action representation (including a controlled gridworld study), context/horizon lengths, and training data scale

Unusually honest reporting of failure modes: underestimation of in-distribution policy values, overestimation for OOD policies, and qualitative failure cases in object interaction physics (Figure 9, 12); limitations section is candid and informative

VLM-as-reward analysis includes useful diagnostics (TP/FP/FN/TN breakdown) and an ablation showing prompt design matters, with low false-positive rates being the desirable property for policy evaluation
weaknesses: The central claim that 'WPE preserves the relative rankings of different policies' is under-supported: only a single learned policy (OpenVLA) is evaluated, and 'ranking' evidence comes from one policy across four tasks plus noisy variants of the same policy; no experiments with multiple genuinely distinct learned policies on the same task, which is the core OPE use case

The OOD results show severe miscalibration (true value 0.09 vs. estimated 0.50 at noise level 0.1), which substantially limits the practical utility of WPE for safety-critical pre-deployment evaluation; the paper treats this as a caveat rather than analyzing its causes or mitigation

The proposed MSE-based world model metric relies on the assumption that transition dynamics are deterministic given actions, but real robot dynamics are stochastic; the reported correlation with human judgment is only ~0.4 (MSE 0.398, SSIM 0.388, LPIPS 0.415), which weakens confidence in all downstream quantitative conclusions built on these metrics

Limited technical novelty in the generative model itself: the architecture is a straightforward combination of DiT, Diffusion Forcing per-token noise levels, and a sliding-window inference scheme similar to Oasis; the 'blockwise autoregressive' scheme is an incremental modification rather than a new method, and there is no comparison against alternative world models or simpler baselines (e.g., next-frame autoregressive prediction, full-sequence diffusion) for the same evaluation task

Real-robot policy evaluation (Section 5.2) is restricted to hard-coded single-axis control policies (gripper open/close, directional sweeps); no learned real-robot policy is evaluated end-to-end, so the headline use case (pre-deployment evaluation of real robot policies) remains largely untested

Statistical rigor is thin: policy value estimates use only 32 trajectories per task with 4 groups for error bars, and VLM reward measurements across 4 runs; given high-variance estimates (e.g., 0.16 ± 0.10), several ranking claims are within noise

Conflating 'ranking across tasks' with 'ranking across policies' is conceptually problematic; task-level differences may reflect world-model fidelity differences per scene rather than policy quality, an alternative explanation not ruled out

Scale is modest for the claims made (609M parameters, 2 A100s for 5 days, 256x256 resolution, 10 sampling steps), and the model's capability ceiling relative to modern video foundation models is not discussed; reproducibility of the full pipeline (OpenX filtering, unified action spaces, GPT-4o reward) is complex and only partially specified

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: using action-conditioned video world models for offline policy evaluation is a relevant and underexplored application, and the paper is, to my knowledge, among the first to quantitatively estimate robot policy success rates with generative video simulators.

The proposed evaluation metrics (semantic MSE over segmented robot arm/object regions conditioned on identical action sequences) are a sensible attempt to measure action-conditioning fidelity, which existing video-generation metrics (FVD, CLIP score) do not capture, and the paper validates them against human judgment.

Useful ablation studies on action representation (raw continuous vectors vs. LLM embeddings), context length, decoding horizon, and dataset scale, including a controlled gridworld experiment; these offer practical guidance for future generative simulators.

The blockwise autoregressive diffusion inference scheme with adjustable context/horizon lengths is a reasonable engineering solution for long-horizon rollouts, and the model is trained with modest resources (609M params, 2xA100 for 5 days), which aids reproducibility.
The paper is commendably honest about limitations, e.g., failure to simulate object interactions and the value-estimation biases.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The world model is essentially Diffusion Forcing [34] + DiT [36] with a sliding-window inference scheme heavily inspired by Oasis [37]; using a VLM (GPT-4o) as a reward/success classifier is also established practice. The core contribution is an empirical study/application rather than a methodological advance.

The central claim — that WPE 'preserves the relative rankings of policies' — is supported by very weak evidence. It is demonstrated on only one base policy (OpenVLA) across 4 LIBERO tasks plus 3 noise-perturbed variants of the same policy. This is far too few and too homogeneous a set of policies to establish ranking preservation; no significance testing or additional policy families are provided.

The quantitative results are quite negative for the method's stated purpose: WPE severely underestimates in-distribution policy values (e.g., 0.47 vs 0.16 on LIBERO-Long) and drastically overestimates out-of-distribution values (0.09 true vs 0.50 estimated at noise 0.1 — a 5x error). AbsolutOPE quality is thus poor, and the paper does not analyze when or why ranking preservation would hold.

Missing baselines. There is no comparison against any existing OPE methods (e.g., FQE, doubly robust estimators, model-based baselines such as Dreamer-style world models, or even a simple next-frame autoregressive baseline without blockwise decoding) that would justify the proposed machinery over alternatives.

The proposed metrics themselves are weak: MSE/SSIM/LPIPS correlate with human judgment at only ~0.39-0.42 (Figure 6), which undermines their use as a reliable evaluation signal for the rest of the paper's conclusions.

Real-robot evaluation is superficial: it is limited to hardcoded single-axis motions and gripper open/close, and the paper's own results show failure to model object interactions (Figure 9, Figure 12), so the claim that WPE can 'sanity check robot policies before deployment' is not convincingly demonstrated for realistic policies.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a top venue: numerous typos ('mimicing', 'Dyanmics', 'looses', 'aboe', 'mean-squred'), an incomplete footnote for the code/videos link, and an incorrect cross-reference (Section 4.2 refers to 'Table 6' when reporting Table 1).

The motivating claim ('there is only one physical world governed by the same set of physical laws', hence one world model can evaluate any policy on any task) is rhetorically appealing but not rigorously argued or tested; the experiments only cover a narrow slice of this claim.

strengths: Timely and clearly motivated research question: whether video world models can serve as simulators for offline policy evaluation of robot policies. This connects the world-modeling literature with the offline policy evaluation literature in a way that has not been systematically studied before, and the paper frames the 'one physical world, many tasks/policies' observation convincingly.

The Blockwise-Autoregressive Diffusion Transformer inference scheme with adjustable context/horizon lengths is a practical contribution that addresses a real problem (fast, low-error-accumulation long-horizon rollouts), building sensibly on Diffusion Forcing while differing in inference.

Comprehensive empirical study across multiple axes: gridworld toy study of action representation, evaluation against a handcrafted simulator (LIBERO) and real-robot data (OpenX/Bridge/RT-1), ablations of context length, horizon length, and training data scale.

The proposed evaluation metrics (semantic MSE via segmentation/tracking, correlation with human judgments) are sensible and address a genuine gap — existing video metrics do not measure action-conditioned fidelity. The paper validates the metrics against human perception.

The findings about underestimating in-distribution and overestimating out-of-distribution policy values, while preserving rankings, are honest and interesting negative results, and the limitations section is candid (object interaction simulation fails).
VLM-as-reward is evaluated quantitatively with TP/FP/FN/TN breakdown, including a useful ablation showing that full-video prompting substantially improves accuracy.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core technical components: the architecture is largely Diffusion Forcing + DiT + Oasis-style latent video diffusion, and the main delta is the blockwise inference scheme. There is no head-to-head comparison against alternative world models (e.g., vanilla next-frame autoregressive, full-sequence diffusion, Diffusion Forcing's original scheme) to demonstrate the claimed advantage in error accumulation and inference speed.

The central practical claim — WPE is useful for pre-deployment policy evaluation — is weakened by the OOD results: WPE significantly overestimates policy values for out-of-distribution policies (e.g., 0.50 vs. 0.09 true value). Overestimating unsafe/novel policies is precisely the failure mode that is dangerous in deployment-time evaluation, and the paper offers no mitigation.

Policy evaluation experiments are limited to a single policy (OpenVLA) on 4 LIBERO tasks and Gaussian-noise-perturbed variants of the same policy; 'preserving rankings' is shown over essentially one monotonic axis, which is weak evidence for the general ranking-preservation claim.

Real-robot evaluation is only qualitative and limited to trivial hard-coded single-dimension controls; no real-world policy value estimation is performed, so the real-robot half of the promise is not quantitatively validated.

Small evaluation samples and moderate metric correlation: 32 rollouts per task with 4 groups for error bars, human-eval correlation of metrics only ~0.4 (MSE 0.398, SSIM 0.388, LPIPS 0.415), which makes the metric-validation argument less compelling than claimed.

Dependence on GPT-4o as the reward function raises reproducibility and cost concerns, and the reward evaluation is on ground-truth videos; the accuracy of the VLM on generated (hallucination-prone) videos is not separately measured, yet VLM errors directly enter the policy-value estimates.

Writing and presentation have numerous errors (e.g., 'mimicing', 'looses', 'aboe', 'Dyanmics', 'mean-squred', dangling footnote for code/videos), and Table 1 is referenced as 'Table 6' in Section 4.2, which slightly undermines polish.
Scale of the world model (609M parameters, 256x256, trained on 2 A100s for 5 days) is modest; claims about the approach's promise are partly extrapolations beyond what this scale demonstrates.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: real-robot policy evaluation is costly, and the paper provides the most comprehensive empirical study to date on whether a video world model can serve as a proxy evaluation environment across robot morphologies (Bridge, RT-1, VIOLA, Berkeley UR5, Google Robot).

The central claim is well supported: a strong correlation (r = 0.78, p < 0.001) between WorldGym and real-world success rates on 17 OpenVLA Bridge tasks, with mean success rates within ~3.3% of real-world values and policy rankings preserved.

The evaluation is thoughtfully layered: (1) world-model agreement with validation split, (2) out-of-distribution end-effector control sweeps showing action controllability beyond training data, (3) correlation with real-world results, (4) ranking preservation across policy versions, sizes, and training checkpoints (including newly trained UniPi and DexVLA-style policies), and (5) OOD image and language evaluations yielding genuinely interesting findings (e.g., policies confusing object shapes, distractor robustness).

The technical design choices are sensible and ablated: Diffusion Forcing with causal temporal attention enables flexible prediction horizon matched to the policy's action chunk size (2.8x speedup shown in Table 9), and action-dropout with CFG improves action adherence.

Good transparency: VLM reward accuracy is validated against ground-truth labels (low false-positive rate), hyperparameters and the rollout algorithm are fully specified, and code/videos are promised; rollouts complete in under an hour on one GPU, demonstrating practicality.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to concurrent/prior work: WorldEval (Li et al., 2025) already evaluates robot policies with a world model, and SIMPLER (Li et al., 2024) achieves highly correlated simulated evaluation; the paper's main new elements (multi-morphology world model, variable horizon alignment, OOD testing) are incremental engineering contributions rather than new methodology.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only 3 main policies, 10 trials per task, and mostly Bridge/Google Robot settings. Per-task success rates are noisy (half-success conventions, e.g., 3.5, 9.5, and half-point partial credits inflate apparent precision), and the ranking-preservation claims largely confirm rankings already known from prior publications, which could plausibly be guessed without the world model.

Potential circularity/confounding: initial frames are taken from the recorded real rollouts of the very policies being evaluated, and the same VLA evaluation suite is used to validate; the paper does not analyze whether world-model artifacts (e.g., object interaction errors the paper itself admits) systematically bias success estimation toward or against particular policy families.

No comparison with baseline evaluation approaches (e.g., SIMPLER, or a simple prediction-error/value-function OPE baseline) on the same suite, so the relative cost/accuracy tradeoff of the proposed approach is not established.

OOD studies are largely qualitative or small-scale (Table 6, 7), and findings like 'OpenVLA struggles to distinguish carrots from oranges by shape' are based on single-scene, single-model experiments with generated images whose fidelity is not validated.

Some overclaiming in framing: 'there is only one physical world' is an intuition rather than a technical argument, and the claim of evaluation on 'novel tasks and environments' relies on GPT-4o rewards whose accuracy was only validated on in-distribution RT-1 videos, not on the OOD or generated-rollout distributions where hallucinated successes may be more likely.

strengths: The core idea — using a single action-conditioned video world model as an offline policy evaluation environment across robot morphologies — is timely, well-motivated, and addresses a genuine bottleneck (costly real-robot evaluation).

The paper validates the world model before using it for evaluation, including action-adherence control sweeps beyond the training distribution and qualitative agreement with real rollouts on Bridge, RT-1, VIOLA, and Berkeley UR5 data.

The diffusion horizon alignment with policy action chunk size is a practical engineering contribution, with a measured 2.8x speedup (Table 9) that supports efficient evaluation of heterogeneous policies.

The OOD experiments (edited images, distractor objects, modified language instructions) demonstrate a genuinely new capability of learned world-model evaluators over handcrafted simulators like SIMPLER, and surface concrete policy failure modes.
Reasonably detailed appendices (hyperparameters, algorithm, VLM prompts, VLM reward validation, dataset ablation) support reproducibility, and code/videos are promised to be released.
weaknesses: The central claim of correlation with real-world success rests on a very small evidence base: only three policies on 17 Bridge tasks, with 10 trials each. The r=0.78 correlation is heavily driven by the fact that OpenVLA (70.6%) is far stronger than RT-1-X and Octo (18-20%); with only three clusters of points, the correlation statistic is fragile and could arise from coarse capability differences rather than faithful dynamics modeling.

Per-task agreement is poor and unexplained: e.g., Lift White Tape (real 1 vs. simulated 6), Lift AAA Battery (7 vs. 4), Put Carrot on Plate (8 vs. 4), Lift White Tape for Octo (0 vs. 1). These are not small deviations, and the paper does not analyze when/why the world model misleads.

The GPT-4o reward model is validated only on real RT-1 videos (Table 3), not on generated world-model rollouts. Reward accuracy on generated videos with visual artifacts is precisely the setting that matters for the claims, and the prompt even instructs the VLM to tolerate generation artifacts — this risks systematically biased success estimation.

Potential data leakage/confounding: the evaluated policies (OpenVLA, Octo, RT-1-X) and the world model are trained on overlapping data (Bridge V2, Open-X), and the policy training-signal experiments (Figure 7) use policies trained on Bridge V2, the same source as the world model. The paper does not discuss how much of the correlation could be explained by shared distribution rather than accurate dynamics.

Object interaction realism is acknowledged as a limitation, yet object manipulation success is the primary metric. Errors in generated object dynamics (e.g., objects teleporting or snapping into place) could inflate or deflate success rates for particular policies in a systematic, policy-dependent way, which is not controlled for.

Comparison with the closest prior work (SIMPLER, WorldEval/Li et al. 2025) is purely qualitative in the related-work section; no head-to-head evaluation on shared tasks is provided, making it hard to assess whether WorldGym is actually more accurate than existing evaluators.

World model quality is only measured with MSE/LPIPS/SSIM and qualitative figures; there is no quantitative metric of action adherence (e.g., end-effector trajectory error between generated and ground-truth videos), so the claim of 'faithfully emulating robot motions' lacks quantitative support.

The training-checkpoint experiments (Figure 7) compare against validation MSE rather than real-world success at each checkpoint, so they demonstrate monotonicity rather than true ranking preservation against real-world ground truth.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence: 'highly correlate' and 'preserved rankings' from three policies and near-chance tasks; 'efficient evaluation' claims rest on a small subset of tasks; the statistical uncertainty of the 10-trial-per-task estimates is substantial relative to many reported differences.

strengths: Timely and practically significant problem: using video world models as evaluation environments for real-robot policies addresses a genuine bottleneck (costly real-world evaluation, sim-to-real gap in handcrafted simulators), and the framing as multi-task offline policy evaluation is well motivated.

Strong empirical validation of the central claim: policy success rates within WorldGym correlate well with real-world success (r = 0.78, p < 0.001), mean success rates differ by only ~3.3% on average, and relative rankings of RT-1-X / Octo / OpenVLA are preserved — supported by a detailed per-task comparison (Table 5).

Comprehensive and multi-pronged evaluation: world model validation via end-effector control sweeps on out-of-distribution action sequences, ranking preservation across policy versions/sizes/training checkpoints, and an interesting OOD study (distractors, unseen objects, OOD language) yielding new findings about VLA failure modes.

Technically sensible design choices with useful ablations: flexible alignment of diffusion prediction horizon with policy action chunk sizes (2.8x speedup shown in Table 9), action dropout with classifier-free guidance for action controllability, and validation of GPT-4o as a reward model with low false positive rate (Table 3).
Reproducibility appears strong: full hyperparameters (Table 2), rollout algorithm (Algorithm 1), VLM prompts, and stated release of videos and code.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the world model is essentially a DiT + Diffusion Forcing combination with an inference-time horizon alignment trick; the main contribution is a system/empirical study rather than a new technique, and concurrent work (WorldEval, SIMPLER, Li et al. 2025) is closely related with no head-to-head quantitative comparison.

Potential circularity in the OOD claims: the world model is trained on Bridge V2 and other Open-X data, so OOD evaluation is done within a simulator whose own competence on edited/novel scenes (e.g., Nano Banana-edited initial frames) is unverified — policy failures observed may reflect world model artifacts rather than true policy weaknesses, and this confound is not adequately controlled or discussed.

Evaluation scale and statistical power are limited: 17 tasks × 10 trials per policy, and per-task agreement is noisy (e.g., Flip Pot Upright 8 vs 5, Lift White Tape 1 vs 6 successes); the r = 0.78 correlation pools 51 points from only 3 policies whose rankings are largely known a priori, so the correlation may overstate per-task predictive reliability.

GPT-4o reward accuracy is validated only on real RT-1 videos, not on generated rollout videos where artifacts are present — yet the reward model is applied exclusively to generated videos; this gap is acknowledged in the prompt but not quantified.

The claim of evaluating 'across different robot morphologies' is somewhat overstated: most quantitative policy evaluation is on Bridge/WidowX with a small Google Robot subset (Appendix E.2), and action-space unification by percentile normalization is coarse.

Some claims rely on weak evidence: ranking preservation across checkpoints (Figure 7) uses only 4 checkpoints per policy with no ground-truth real-robot comparison for those checkpoints, only validation MSE as a proxy.
